title: Bringing work back together
objective: By the end of this lesson you can merge a branch deliberately, read the two shapes a merge can take, and know what to check before merging anything into a shared branch.

blocks.text: A branch that is never merged is a branch that did nothing. Merging takes the commits from one line of work and brings them into another. The command is short; the useful knowledge is what Git does with it and what you should look at first.

blocks.caption: The direction matters
lines: git switch main               # go to the branch that will RECEIVE the work
git merge feature/upload      # bring that branch's commits into main
# You always merge FROM a branch INTO the one you are standing on.

blocks.text: Two shapes a merge can take
Which one you get is decided by whether the receiving branch moved on while you were away. Both are normal.

blocks.caption: Fast-forward: main did not move
lines: # Git just slides the label forward. No merge commit is needed.

blocks.caption: Merge commit: both branches moved
lines: after:    a1 ── b2 ── e5 ──── m6  ← main
# m6 is a merge commit: it has two parents and joins the two lines.

blocks.title: A merge commit is not clutter
blocks.text: It records a true fact — that two lines of development came together at this point, and which two. Teams that ban merge commits entirely lose that information; teams that produce them for every tiny change make the history hard to read. A common middle ground: merge commits for real branches, tidy history within a branch.
What to do before merging into a shared branch

items: Update the receiving branch first, so you are merging into today's state, not last week's
Read what is actually coming: git log main..feature and git diff main...feature
Run the tests on the merged result, not just on your branch in isolation
Merge, then confirm the receiving branch still works before anyone else pulls it

blocks.caption: The check that prevents most bad merges
lines: git switch main && git pull        # today's state
git log --oneline main..feature    # commits that are about to arrive
git diff main...feature            # the actual change, in full
# run the tests here — a merge can break things neither branch broke alone

blocks.title: Two clean branches can still produce a broken result
blocks.text: One branch renames a function, another adds a new call to the old name. Neither branch is wrong on its own and there is no textual conflict, so the merge succeeds — and the result does not work. This is why the tests matter after the merge, not only before it.

rows: Fast-forward if possible, otherwise a merge commit
You want the branch visible as a unit in the history
Bring the changes in as one uncommitted change
Many small messy commits you do not want to preserve
Return to the state before you started
A conflicted merge you would rather redo later

blocks.title: Produce both merge shapes on purpose
steps: In ~/git-lab: git switch -c feature/one && echo one > one.txt && git add . && git commit -m "Add one"
Run: git switch main && git merge feature/one     (fast-forward — no merge commit)
Run: git switch -c feature/two && echo two > two.txt && git add . && git commit -m "Add two"
Run: git switch main && echo main-side >> notes.txt && git commit -am "Change on main"
Run: git merge feature/two                        (now a merge commit is required)
blocks.expected: The first merge moves the label with no extra commit; the second creates a merge commit joining two lines. Seeing both once is enough to recognise them in any repository afterwards.

cheatsheet: Merge FROM a branch INTO the one you are standing on — switch first
Fast-forward: the receiving branch did not move, so the label slides forward
Merge commit: both moved, so a commit with two parents joins them
Update the receiving branch before merging into it
git log main..feature — what commits are about to arrive
git diff main...feature — the full change being merged
Run tests AFTER the merge: two clean branches can still combine into a broken result
--no-ff forces a merge commit · --squash collapses to one change · --abort backs out

checkpoint.prompt: You want to bring feature/upload into main. What is the correct sequence?

choices.A: git switch feature/upload then git merge main
choices.B: git switch main then git merge feature/upload
choices.C: git merge main feature/upload from anywhere
choices.D: git switch main then git merge --abort

checkpoint.explanation: You stand on the branch that receives the work, then merge the other one into it. Doing it the other way round brings main's commits into the feature branch instead.

checkpoint.prompt: When does Git produce a merge commit rather than a fast-forward?

choices.A: Whenever more than one file changed
choices.B: When the receiving branch also gained commits since the other branch split off
choices.C: Only when there is a conflict

checkpoint.explanation: If the receiving branch has not moved, the label can simply slide forward. If both moved, a commit with two parents is needed to join them.

checkpoint.prompt: Two branches merge with no conflicts, but the application is broken afterwards. How?

choices.A: That cannot happen — no conflict means a safe merge
choices.B: Changes can be textually compatible but semantically incompatible — one branch renames something the other branch started calling
choices.D: The merge commit overwrote the tests

checkpoint.explanation: Git compares text, not meaning. This is exactly why the test run belongs after the merge as well as before it.

checkpoint.prompt: What does git merge --squash feature do?

choices.A: Deletes the feature branch after merging
choices.B: Brings the branch's changes in as a single uncommitted change, discarding its individual commits

checkpoint.explanation: It is the option for a branch full of small messy commits whose individual steps are not worth keeping in the shared history.
